name: Chaudangsi
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Krishan, Shree. 2001. A Sketch of Chaudangsi Grammar. In Yasuhiko Nagano & Randy J. LaPolla (eds), New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages (Bon Studies 3; Senri Ethnological Reports 19), 401-448. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology. doi:10.15021/00002152
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: Harvard print copy (Scan & Deliver or loan); the journal or volume is held, not the item itself: TOZ Offsite Storage MUS.69.80.1.4 (19)
sources.note: Phonology 2.0-2.8 (pp. 402-408) read in full: inventories, contrasts, clusters, vowel sequences, syllable structure, five phonological rules. No stress, accent, tone or pitch statement anywhere (grep stress/accent/tone/pitch/prominen/suprasegm/intonation = 0 hits). Only prosodic remarks: 2.7 'Chaudangsi is basically a monosyllabic language'; 2.8(i) 'If two or more phonetically long vowels occur in successive syllables, the first one is shortened.'

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Chaudangsi language' (refs: Ethnologue 2015, S.R. Sharma 2001, Atkinson 1882, Walton 1911, Benedict 1972)
Krishan, Shree. 2001. A Sketch of Darma Grammar. Same volume, 347-400. (sister language Darmiya darm1243, read only as a methodology check)
sources.note: Has sec. 2.2 'Tones' (three marginal lexical tones, left unmarked) but no stress statement for Darma; shows the author writes a suprasegmental section when he finds something, and the Chaudangsi sketch has none. Not about Chaudangsi.

sources.citation: Krishan, Shree. 2001. Darma, Chaudangsi, and Raji. In Nagano & LaPolla (eds), New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages (SER 19), 343-345. doi:10.15021/00002150
sources.note: Ethnographic/sociolinguistic overview only. p. 345: 'the phonology and skeleton grammars of Darma and Chaudangsi have been worked out. However, these are in no way comprehensive studies of either language.' Nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: LaPolla, Randy J. (ed.). 2001 [Glottolog lists it as 2003]. The Tibeto-Burman Languages of Uttar Pradesh. City University of Hong Kong (compiled volume, 279 pp.); Krishan, Shree, 'A Sketch of Chaudangsi Grammar', pp. 175-196, glossaries 197-215 (pdf page 191).
sources.note: Same text and section structure (2.0-2.8) as the SER19 version; no stress/accent/tone statement in the Chaudangsi chapter (grep = 0 hits). fetched sources from https://randylapolla.info/Papers/; Glottolog's tibeto-burman.net URL is dead (host times out; the single Wayback capture of 2019-12-11 is a GoDaddy parking page).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.; section by Sten Konow). 1909. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. III Part I: Tibeto-Burman Family. Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing. 'Chaudangsi', pp. 503ff.
sources.note: 'Pronunciation' paragraph covers vowel length, dropped final vowels/consonants, simplified clusters; then p. 504: 'There is no indication of the existence of tones in the materials available.' No accent or stress statement. Based on written specimens by Babu Gobind Prasad, 'given with some reserve'.

sources.citation: Sharma, D. D. 1989. Chaudangsi-Byangsi. In Tibeto-Himalayan Languages of Uttarakhand, Part One (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages III), 101-194. New Delhi: Mittal Publications. ISBN 81-7099-...; OCLC 636780037
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: The other first-hand sketch of the language (treats Chaudangsi and Byangsi as one dialect). Sibling chapters in the same Mittal series carry an 'Accent' subsection (the Jad chapter, Part Two p. 18, states initial-syllable stress), so this chapter is the most likely place for an explicit Chaudangsi-Byangsi stress statement.

sources.citation: Sharma, Suhnu Ram. 2007. Byangsi Grammar and Vocabulary. Pune: Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Modern grammar of Byangsi; per Willis's 2009 review (on file in../byan1241) it describes a three-way tone contrast and 'does not mention the stress pattern found in Byangsi', so it likely does not settle stress even for the sister variety, but it is the only recent book-length treatment of the Byangsi-Chaudangsi dialect cluster.

sources.citation: Trivedi, G. M. 1991. Descriptive Grammar of Byansi. Calcutta: Anthropological Survey of India. 233 pp.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Fullest grammar of the sister variety Byangsi, which LSI 1909 calls 'almost one and the same dialect' as Chaudangsi; a stress section there would be the closest proxy. Not a Chaudangsi description proper.
